13128-corea-or-cho-sen-the-land-of-the-m:
A. Henry Savage-Landor's 1895 travel book on Korea, then called Corea or Cho-sen, draws on his own drawings and journeys. He dedicates it to Queen Victoria and moves from Christmas aboard ship at Fusan through Chemulpo to Seoul and the court. Chapters cover cotton, body-snatching tales, hotels, Japanese concessions, and Korean history.

Savage-Landor recounts a tug-of-war over a child, sedan chairs waiting for officials, and a prince's court where he removed his shoes before entering. His tone is that of a confident Victorian traveler, curious and often blunt. The book gives a detailed, if dated, view of Korea just before its world changed fast.
18714-abe-and-mawruss-being-further-adve:
Montague Glass returned to his famous partners in this 1911 Doubleday collection, further adventures of Potash and Perlmutter. Abe Potash and Morris Perlmutter run their showroom with endless talk, sharp bargains, and warm quarrels, rendered in the partners' own comic dialect.

Stories with titles like Sympathy, The Judgment of Paris, The Raincoat King, and Firing Miss Cohen follow them through customers, rivals, and family claims on their time and money. The opening tale turns on Abe's praise of a supposed philanthropist, which Mawruss gleefully cuts down to mere talkativeness. Glass makes business comedy from two men who can sell anything except, sometimes, each other.
20347-the-moving-picture-girls-snowbound:
Laura Lee Hope published The Moving Picture Girls Snowbound in 1914. Alice DeVere, rather plump, with dark brown hair and eyes, waits at home. Her fairness contrasts with her sister Ruth's looks, the book notes. Their father is more than an hour late from the moving picture studio.

He promised to be back at four, and now it is after five. The Moving Picture Girls act in early films while storms trap them. Snowbound tales strand their cast far from the studio's bright lights. Young readers get early cinema glamor mixed with winter adventure.
2289-rosmersholm:
Henrik Ibsen's Rosmersholm stages a political and moral crisis in a Norwegian manor haunted by its past. Johannes Rosmer, a former pastor, has left the church and embraced free thought, but guilt over his wife's death and the scheming of Rebecca West pull him toward ruin. Ibsen's four-act play works through whispers, confessions, and the weight of a house's traditions.

The drama's power lies in what is not said: old sins, hidden motives, and the price of a clear conscience. Rosmer and Rebecca's final walk to the millrace is among Ibsen's most famous closes. Readers of serious drama will find a play of great psychological depth.
23361-pe-re-antoine-s-date-palm:
Thomas Bailey Aldrich built this New Orleans tale around a tall date palm near the levee, by the old French cathedral in the Place d'Armes. Sir Charles Lyell had noted the tree, some seventy or eighty years old, planted in youth by Pere Antoine, a Catholic priest who guarded it in his will.

Aldrich traces the priest's later life, as the old man grew thin and dry, walking the streets like a mummy, and the Creole folk who recalled him. The palm, with its broad leaves in alien air, becomes a sign of faith, age, and rootedness far from home. The tale is short and wistful, blending local lore, a real tree, and a priest whose life seemed to mirror the plant he loved.
23741-david-malcolm:
Nelson Lloyd published David Malcolm with Scribner's in 1913, dedicating it to his wife Susanne Livingston Green Lloyd, who worked with him over its pages. Its narrator is David himself, an only child under a double portion of maternal care. The book opens with his mother warning him from the gate not to tumble into the water.

David, perched on the back of the off-wheeler with boyish self-assurance, folds his arms like a circus rider rather than hold the harness. A second warning follows, about rattlesnakes, and a surreptitious kick fails to move the horse. From such small boyhood scenes Lloyd builds a novel of growing up, family, and a young man's push toward self-reliance.
3818-by-reef-and-palm:
Louis Becke, once a trader running a cutter between Apia and Savaii, writes these South Sea tales from first hand knowledge. The introduction recalls October 1870 in Apia, Samoa, when German traders feared a French squadron and the beach still buzzed over the pirate Pease and the notorious Bully Hayes. Becke's stories follow traders, chiefs, and beachcombers through love, revenge, and sudden fortune.

Challis the doubter, Macy O'Shea's revenge, the rangers of Tia Kau, and Enderby's courtship fill the contents. A Gilbert Islands village scene shows how a name shouted through a town house stops all song. Becke writes plainly and without polish, which suits his rough material. Readers who like island adventure will find a book salted with real Pacific life.
44404-adrift-in-the-unknown-or-queer-adv:
William Wallace Cook wrote Adrift in the Unknown, or Queer Adventures in a Queer Realm, a dime novel from the Munsey magazines, reissued by Street and Smith. Cook's name fills the Adventure Library. For the present, the publishers say, the whole library will be devoted to his stories, each different in plot and locality.

Contents open with lost, strayed, or stolen, then an uninvited guest and a professor's feat. The plutocrats are reconciled, and the party travels sunward. A landing is effected, a Mercurial storm faced, and the Mercurials met. Cook, who plotted novels by a mechanical system of cards, sent his castaways to Mercury when interplanetary tales were new.
51367-poems-pastoral-and-psalm:
Poems: Pastoral and Psalm is a volume of verse by the Rev Benjamin Copeland. Eaton and Mains published it in New York in 1896, with Curts and Jennings in Cincinnati. The opening poem, The First Robin, hails the redbreast as herald of the happy year. Age and childhood, the poem says, find a kindred bond in the bird. His song turns winter's dearth to summer's dower.

The Meadow Air Is Sweet follows, built on a repeated first line. Its stanzas pass from cowslip and blackbird to clover, daisy, and swallow. A Contrast sets the green silence of a sylvan shore against the city's roar. The Goal seeks repose among sweet scents and solemn silences. Copeland's poems join pastoral description to churchly feeling. Nature's Easter festival, as the robin poem calls spring, is his constant theme.
64852-george-helm:
David Graham Phillips wrote this novel, published in New York in September 1912, months after the author's death. Phillips was a muckraking journalist whose novels attacked money and power in American life. A list of his works fronts the book, from The Deluge to The Great God Success.

The contents open with a chapter called Behind the Beard, then move to The Cat's-Paw and a chapter titled simply There Goes a Man. George Helm stands at the center of a tale of ambition and the price of success. Phillips writes with a reporter's speed and a reformer's anger. Readers get a late work from a novelist who helped stir a nation's conscience.
6863-the-passing-of-new-france-a-chronic:
William Wood tells the passing of New France in a chronicle of Montcalm, volume ten of the Chronicles of Canada, Toronto, 1915. War is the grave of the Montcalms, an old saying runs, as old as France herself, for Montcalm-Gozon men were always ready to fight for king and country. Montcalm, like Wolfe, was a soldier born, with ancestors famous in the Crusades.

Chapter one follows Montcalm in France from 1712 to 1756, before his Canadian campaigns and his death at Quebec. Wood writes with a historian's clarity and a storyteller's pace. The Passing of New France is a vivid, classic chronicle of a lost French empire.
70417-tinting-and-toning-of-eastman-posi:
The Eastman Kodak Company put out this guide to the tint and tone of film, in a fresh shape of 1918. Its price was two coins and a half. In the make of film for the screen it grows more and more the wont, the book says, to shift the hue of the film. That shift is made by tone, by tint, or by a mix of the two ways. The book tells what each way is, and how each is done.

To tone is to swap the image of black ore, in whole or in part, for a stuff of a set hue. The clear parts of the frame, which are plain gum, are left bare of hue. To tint is to dip the film in a bath of dye.
7127-malcolm:
George MacDonald's Malcolm opens with a long roll of contents, from Miss Horn and Barbara Catanach through the mad laird, Phemy Mair, and Lady Florimel. Duncan MacPhail, Alexander Graham, the swivel, and the salmon trout follow, with a funeral, the old church, and the churchyard. The Marquis of Lossie, Meg Partan's lamp, the slope of the dune, and the storm lead to accusation, quarrel, and Duncan's pipes.

Advances, mediation, whence and whither, Armageddon, and the feast follow, with a night watch, not at church, and Lord Gernon. A fisher wedding, Florimel and Duncan, and a revival precede wandering stars, the skipper's chamber, and the library. Milton and the bay mare, Kirkbyres, the blow, and the cutter carry the tale toward Colonsay Castle and the deil's winnock.
71747-the-film:
Jackson Wrigley wrote a book on how film can teach the great crowd. Wrigley was chief book man at the Liverpool Library. Gilbert Parker wrote a front note for the book. Walter Briscoe of Nottingham wrote its first words as well. The book came out in London and New York in 1922.

Wrigley gave the book to two dead mates of the book world. Both fell for their land in France in the Great War. Parts of the book first ran as talks and papers, he says. He holds film a firm ally for schools and book houses. How to pick, show, and use films fills his plan. Book and school men get a new tool's case.
abe-and-mawruss-being-further-adventures: Montague Glass tells further adventures of Potash and Perlmutter in Abe and Mawruss, published by Doubleday, Page in 1911. The contents run from Sympathy and The Judgment of Paris through Dead Men's Shoes and The Raincoat King to A Return to Arcady. A Present for Geigermann, Brothers All, and others follow, with Firing Miss Cohen, Aux Italiens, and Man Proposes closing the book. The frontispiece praises being up to date in business.
britannica-1911-anselm:
Anselm, who lived from about 1033 to 1109, was archbishop of Canterbury. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica opens with his birth at Aosta in Piedmont. His father was a Lombard of harsh and violent temper. His mother, a prudent woman, trained him in the faith. At fifteen he wished to enter a convent, but his father refused. Sickness and then a gay worldly spell followed that check.

His mother's death and his father's harshness drove him from home. He crossed the Alps and wandered France with one attendant. The fame of Lanfranc drew him to the monastery of Bec. At twenty seven he became a monk there. Three years later he was made prior, and in 1078 abbot. Under him Bec became the first seat of learning in Europe. In those quiet years he wrote his famed works. The Monologion and Proslogion date from that abbacy.
britannica-1911-augusti-johann-christian:
Johann Christian Wilhelm Augusti (1772-1841) was a German church scholar, treated in this 1911 Britannica article. Born at Eschenberga near Gotha, he was of Jewish descent, his grandfather having been a rabbi who changed faith. He studied at Gotha and at Jena, where he became a teacher of eastern tongues in 1803.

Augusti later held chairs at Breslau and then at Bonn, and in 1828 joined the church council at Coblenz, where he died. The article says he kept to the old faith while still judging the Bible tales with a free mind. His books include a history of church teaching, a new version of the Old Testament made with de Wette in 1809, and large works on early church remains and rites.
britannica-1911-balm:
Balm is a sweet-smelling herb, Melissa officinalis, of the deadnettle family. It has opposite, egg-shaped leaves with toothed edges, wrinkled on top, and small white or rose-spotted flowers. The plant is native to central and southern Europe.

Gardeners often grow it, and it has spread as a garden escape in the south of England and in North America. Its name comes from the Greek word for a bee, since bees visit it freely. The 1911 Britannica entry closes with a near kin, bastard balm, an allied plant of southern Europe also found in the south and south-west of England.
britannica-1911-bessel-friedrich-wilhelm:
Friedrich Wilhelm Bessel (1784–1846) was a German astronomer, born at Minden. At fifteen he entered a counting house at Bremen. Hopes of a post on a foreign voyage led him to navigation, mathematics, and astronomy. In 1804 he worked out the orbit of Halley's comet from old observations. Olbers printed the result and won him an observatory post at Lilienthal. A study of the comet of 1807 raised his name further.

In 1810 the king of Prussia called him to build a new observatory at Königsberg. He directed it from 1813 until his death. The 1911 Britannica entry credits him with opening the modern era of practical astronomy. He cut Bradley's Greenwich observations into a catalogue of 3,222 stars, the Fundamenta Astronomiae of 1818. His tables and perturbation studies fill the entry's close.
britannica-1911-bristow-benjamin-helm:
Benjamin Helm Bristow (1832–1896) was an American lawyer and politician born in Elkton, Kentucky, on 20 June 1832, son of a Whig congressman. He graduated at Jefferson College, Canonsburg, in 1851, studied law under his father and joined the Kentucky bar in 1853. War service and federal law posts built his career step by step.

In the Civil War he rose to colonel of the 8th Kentucky Cavalry, was badly wounded at Shiloh and helped capture John H. Morgan in July 1863. State senator in 1863-1865, federal district attorney for Louisville from 1866 to 1870, he then became the first appointed solicitor-general of the United States. As secretary of the treasury from 1874 to 1876 he prosecuted with vigour the Whisky Ring centred at St Louis, the fight that dominates the later part of the account.
britannica-1911-brunswick-bevern-august-:
August Wilhelm, Duke of Brunswick-Bevern (1715–1781), was a Prussian soldier, son of Ernst Ferdinand, duke of Brunswick-Bevern, born at Brunswick in 1715. He entered the Prussian army in 1731, became colonel of an infantry regiment in 1739, won great distinction at Hohenfriedeberg as a major-general, and was promoted lieutenant-general in 1750. Frederick the Great's army held few soldiers more experienced or exact.

He commanded a wing at Lobositz in 1756 and beat the Austrians under Marshal Konigsegg at Reichenberg on 21 April 1757 in a well-fought battle. After fighting at Prague and Kolin and the retreat to Gorlitz, he commanded the Prussians Frederick left behind in autumn 1757 during the march against the French. His defensive campaign against overwhelming numbers showed great skill, but General Winterfeld's death in a skirmish at Moys cost him dear.
britannica-1911-coco-nut-palm:
Coco-nut palm, known in science as Cocos nucifera, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is a tall and graceful palm that grows from sixty to one hundred feet high. Its round stem can reach two feet thick. At the top spreads a crown of waving leaves split like feathers.

Each leaf can reach twenty feet long, with a strong mid rib and many long sharp leaflets. That build gives the leaf the look of a giant feather. Flowers grow in branching spikes five or six feet long inside a tough sheath. Fruits ripen in bunches of ten to twenty. Each ripe fruit runs twelve to eighteen inches long, with a thick fibrous husk around the hard nut of commerce.
britannica-1911-culm:
Culm, in geology, names a local phase of the Carboniferous system, dark shales, grits, and impure limestones in Devon and the counties near it. Sedgwick and Murchison split the beds into Upper and Lower Culm Measures in 1837. The name came from impure coals, locally called culm, in the shales near Bideford. The same name was later carried to like rocks in Germany and Austria. A shared fossil shell, Posidonomya Becheri, linked the two fields.

The Devon beds lie folded in a broad trough, much crushed and hard to read. Ussher later split them into Upper, Middle, and Lower measures. Arber showed from fossil plants that the Upper Culm matches the Middle Coal Measures of other parts of Britain. No fossil split of the upper beds proved possible. Lists of index fossils, from Glyphioceras to Lepidodendron, support the dating. A full bibliography of the English Culm closes the entry.
britannica-1911-date-palm:
The date palm is the tree whose fruit forms the dates of trade. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives its range from the Canary Islands to India. It crosses north Africa and the south east of Asia. Peoples have grown and prized it from the remotest ages. Assyrian wall tablets show its care in old times. In Arabia it is the chief source of national wealth. Its fruit is the staple food of that land.

Spanish missionaries carried it to the New World in early days. The tree rises 60 to 80 feet on a scarred stem, topped by shining feather leaves. Male and female flowers grow on separate trees. Growers must thus dust the female blooms by hand. The fruit is oblong and fleshy, with one very hard seed.
britannica-1911-elm:
Elm is the popular name for the trees and shrubs of the genus Ulmus, in the natural order Ulmaceae. The genus holds fifteen or sixteen species spread through the north temperate zone, except for western North America. It reaches south as far as Mexico and the Sikkim Himalayas. The entry describes the common elm in most detail.

The common elm, Ulmus campestris, is a doubtful native of England and grows across much of Europe, North Africa, and Asia Minor to Japan. It reaches 60 to 100 feet, and sometimes 150 feet, flowering before the leaves in March and April. In England it rarely ripens its seed and is raised from root suckers or layers. Its wood is close-grained, hard, and tough, and lasts well under water, though it decays fast in open weather. The entry also treats the wych elm, the Dutch elm, and the American or white elm of Boston Common.
britannica-1911-ernst-heinrich-wilhelm:
Ernst, Heinrich Wilhelm (1814–1865), was a German violinist and composer born at Brünn in Moravia in 1814. He was educated at the Conservatorium of Vienna, studying the violin under Joseph Böhm and Joseph Mayseder, and composition under Ignaz von Seyfried. At sixteen he made a concert tour in south Germany. 

In 1832 Ernst went to Paris, where he lived for several years and grew close to Stephen Heller; their joint Pensées fugitives for piano and violin came from that friendship. He first visited London in 1843, and the strong impression he made was more than confirmed the next year. The last seven years of his life were spent in retirement, chiefly at Nice, where he died on 8 October 1865. The entry praises his almost unrivalled power of execution, his loftiness of conception, and his passionate expression. His Elegie and Otello Fantasia rank among the most treasured works for the violin.
britannica-1911-freund-wilhelm:
Wilhelm Freund (1806-1894), German scholar of language and maker of dictionaries, was born at Kempen in Posen on 27 January 1806. He studied at Berlin, Breslau, and Halle, then spent twenty years mainly in private tuition. From 1855 to 1870 he directed the Jewish school at Gleiwitz in Silesia, then retired to Breslau, where he died on 4 June 1894.

Freund also worked hard for the civil freedom of his fellow Jews in Prussia, and the Judengesetz of 1847 owed much to his efforts. His lasting work is the Wörterbuch der lateinischen Sprache, issued from 1834 to 1845, which the entry calls practically the basis of all Latin-English dictionaries. His guides for students of classical philology also ran to several editions. The hosted file also holds the neighbouring entries for Fresno, Fret, and Freudenstadt.
britannica-1911-gade-niels-wilhelm:
Gade, Niels Wilhelm (1817–1890), a Danish composer, was born at Copenhagen on the 22nd of February 1817, the son of a musical instrument maker. Meant for his father's trade, he forced his own way into music and was largely self-taught, though he played in the court band. His Ossian overture of 1841 won the local musical society's prize and a royal stipend that sent him to Leipzig and Italy. In 1844 he conducted the Gewandhaus concerts during Mendelssohn's absence, and on Mendelssohn's death he became chief conductor.

In 1848 the Holstein war brought him home to Copenhagen, where he became organist, conductor of the Musik-Verein and, in 1861, court conductor. His eight symphonies, best in the first and fourth, show a romantic gift polished and lyrical rather than dramatic. Works such as The Crusaders, Frühlingsfantasie and Psyche, written for Birmingham in 1882, won wide popularity. He died at Copenhagen on the 21st of December 1890.
britannica-1911-gotter-friedrich-wilhelm:
Friedrich Wilhelm Gotter, a German poet and playwright who lived from 1746 to 1797, is covered in a 1911 Britannica life story. He was born at Gotha on September 3, 1746. After his years at Gottingen he worked in the town archive. He later served at Wetzlar, seat of the imperial law courts.

In 1768 Gotter came back to Gotha as a tutor and helped found a famed book of poems. At Wetzlar he moved in Goethe's circle. He stood as the chief voice of French taste in German letters of his time. His verse is praised as smooth and neat, though lacking depth. His plays, most drawn from French works, pushed back on wild new drama.
britannica-1911-gottling-carl-wilhelm:
Carl Wilhelm Gottling (1793-1869) was a German classical scholar, born at Jena on 19 January 1793. The 1911 Britannica entry has him studying at Jena and Berlin, fighting against France in 1814, and settling in 1822 as professor at his native town's university. He stayed there until his death on 20 January 1869.

His early work was German: two books on the Nibelungen, in 1814 and 1817. The greater part of his life went to Greek authors. He edited Theodosius's grammar, Aristotle's Politics and Economics, and Hesiod. His study of Greek accent, enlarged in 1835, reached English readers as the Elements of Greek Accentuation. The entry lists his collected papers and his correspondence with Goethe, published in 1880. Colleagues' memoirs of him are named at the close.
britannica-1911-heinse-johann-jakob-wilh:
Johann Jakob Wilhelm Heinse (1749–1803) was a German author. He was born at Langewiesen in Thuringia on 16 February 1749. Schleusingen's gymnasium schooled him before law at Jena and Erfurt. Wieland's acquaintance at Erfurt changed his path. Gleim procured him a tutorship at Quedlinburg in 1772. Düsseldorf took him in 1774 to help edit the Iris periodical. Its picture gallery fired his passion for art.

Jacobi funded three years of Italian study for him, 1780 to 1783. In 1786 the elector of Mainz made him his reader. Librarian at Aschaffenburg was his later post there. He died at Aschaffenburg on 22 June 1803. His fame rests on Ardinghello und die glückseligen Inseln (1787). That novel frames his views on art and life in 16th-century Italy. Wieland's frankness and Sturm und Drang enthusiasm mix in his work. The romantic school felt his influence strongly.
britannica-1911-hengstenberg-ernst-wilhe:
Ernst Wilhelm Hengstenberg (1802–1869) was a German Lutheran divine. He was born at Fröndenberg in Westphalia in October 1802. His father, a Reformed pastor, taught him at home. Bonn took him in as a student in 1819. He gave his time to tongues, church past and thought. His text of Amru'l-Qais won the prize at his degree. A German form of Aristotle's Metaphysics came in 1824. Basel then gave him work as a tutor in Eastern tongues.

Bible study at Basel fixed his faith for life. Berlin took him as a young teacher in 1824. His theses of 1825 fought all forms of rational thought in faith. Old Testament doubts were his chief mark. In 1827 he took charge of a strict church paper. It won a name almost without match in his hands. His Christology of the Old Testament began in 1828. He died on 28 May 1869.
britannica-1911-hinrichs-hermann-friedri:
Hermann Friedrich Wilhelm Hinrichs (1794–1861) was a German thinker. He studied theology at Strassburg and thought at Heidelberg under Hegel. Hegel wrote a preface to his book on religion and science, printed at Heidelberg. Hinrichs became a teacher in 1819 and held chairs at Breslau in 1822 and at Halle in 1824. By his works he became a known voice of the strict school of Hegel.

His books fall in three sets in the article. The books on thought include a work on the ground lines of logic and a Genesis of Knowledge. The books on art include talks on Goethe's Faust and a work on the poems of Schiller in their past setting. The books on history include a work on law and state rules since the Reformation, in three parts from 1848 to 1852, and a work called Die Könige.
britannica-1911-hufeland-christoph-wilhe:
Christoph Wilhelm Hufeland (1762-1836) was a German physician, and his career is set out in an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Langensalza, he was educated at Weimar, where his father was court physician. He graduated in medicine at Goettingen in 1783 and helped his father for some years.

The entry says he was called to the chair of medicine at Jena in 1793, then in 1798 put at the head of state medical affairs in Berlin. He is honored as the most eminent practical physician of his time in Germany. His best known work, on the art of lengthening human life, was translated into many languages.
britannica-1911-iffland-august-wilhelm:
Iffland, August Wilhelm is a life story from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a German actor and playwright. He was born at Hanover on the nineteenth of April 1759 and died in 1814. His father meant him for the church. At eighteen the boy ran away to Gotha to train for the stage.

There he was lucky to learn from Hans Ekhof, and he grew so fast that Mannheim took him on in 1779. Soon he stood high in his craft and played in many towns. In 1796 he settled in Berlin as head of the Prussian national theatre. In 1811 he became general director of all shows before royalty. He staged Goethe and Schiller with great care. His own home ground, as actor and writer alike, was the domestic drama of daily life.
britannica-1911-kalkbrenner-friedrich-wi:
Friedrich Wilhelm Kalkbrenner (1784–1849) was a German pianist and composer, son of Christian Kalkbrenner, a Jewish musician of Cassel. He was trained at the Paris Conservatoire and soon began to play in public. From 1814 to 1823 he was well known in London as a brilliant player and a successful teacher, and then he settled in Paris.

He became a member of the Paris piano making firm of Pleyel and Company, and made a fortune from trade and art together. He died at Enghien, near Paris, in 1849. His many compositions are less remembered now than his instruction book. Its studies have had a wide vogue among pianists. The entry is a short life: training, two capitals, a trade in pianos, and the teaching book that kept his name alive.
britannica-1911-lachmann-karl-konrad-fri:
Karl Konrad Friedrich Wilhelm Lachmann (1793–1851), German philologist and critic, was born at Brunswick on the 4th of March 1793 and studied at Leipzig and Göttingen. In 1815 he served as a volunteer chasseur with the Prussian army in Paris. He taught in Berlin gymnasia, then at Königsberg helped Köpke edit Rudolf von Ems and planned an edition of Walther von der Vogelweide. In January 1818 he became professor of classical philology at Königsberg and lectured on Old German grammar and the Middle High German poets.

After seven years of close study he took leave in 1824 to search the libraries of middle and south Germany. He then moved to Berlin as professor of classical and German philology in 1825, becoming ordinary professor in 1827 and joining the Academy of Sciences in 1830. His editions include the Auswahl of 1820, Hartmann's Iwein (1827), Walther (1827) and Wolfram von Eschenbach (1833). He died on the 13th of March 1851.
britannica-1911-laing-malcolm:
Malcolm Laing (1762–1818), Scottish historian, was born on the Mainland of Orkney, the elder brother of Samuel Laing the elder. He studied at Kirkwall grammar school and Edinburgh University and was called to the Scotch bar in 1785, but gave his time chiefly to historical studies. In 1793 he completed the sixth and last volume of Robert Henry's History of Great Britain, in a liberal tone.

In 1802 he published his History of Scotland, from the Union of the Crowns to the Union of the Kingdoms. It carried dissertations on the Gowrie conspiracy and on the authenticity of Ossian's poems. For the second edition of 1804 he added a dissertation that Mary, queen of Scots, wrote the Casket Letters and shared in the murder of Darnley. He edited the Life and Historie of King James VI and sat as member of parliament for Orkney and Shetland from 1807 to 1812. He died on the 6th of November 1818.
britannica-1911-langholm:
Langholm is a small burgh in Dumfriesshire, Scotland. It stands on both banks of the Esk. Annan lies some 16 miles to the south-west. A three-arched stone bridge joins old town and new. A branch rail line links the place to Riddings Junction. The count for 1901 gave 3,142 people.

The town hall has a tiered tower. The Telford library stands nearby. A hospital serves aged poor. Plaids and blankets made the town's name first. Tweed making then lifted its trade. Distilling, brewing, dyeing, and tanning also went on. Nearby stand Langholm Lodge and Gilnockie Tower. That tower once held Johnny Armstrong, the freebooter.
britannica-1911-maccoll-malcolm:
Malcolm MacColl, British clergyman and writer on public affairs, lived from about 1838 to 1907 and is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a son of a Scottish farmer. Training at Trinity College at Glenalmond fit him for the Scotch Episcopal ministry. More study at Naples came before his ordination in 1859.

Curacies in London and at Addington in Bucks came next for him. He soon won note as a fighter in print on church and state. His pen backed Gladstone, who gave him a London living in 1871 and a canonry of Ripon in 1884. Wide travel in Europe fed his pamphlets and press letters. He spoke out with force on the Eastern Question and on the wrongs claimed in Bulgaria and Armenia.
britannica-1911-malcolm:
Malcolm is the subject of a kings article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The name was borne by four kings of the Scots. The first two, who ruled in the nine hundreds and early ten hundreds, are called shadowy and minor figures. The article gives most space to Malcolm the Third, who died in 1093.

Malcolm the Third, called Canmore, was a son of King Duncan the First. He became king after the defeat of Macbeth and was crowned at Scone in 1057. He raided the north of England again and again to back a claim to its throne. He made peace with William the Conqueror, then broke it. He was killed near Alnwick in 1093 while raiding south once more. Four of his sons later ruled Scotland. The last king, Malcolm the Fourth, is treated in brief.
britannica-1911-ramler-karl-wilhelm:
Karl Wilhelm Ramler is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Ramler was a German poet, born at Kolberg in 1725. After his studies at Halle he settled in Berlin. In 1748 he became professor of logic and literature at the cadet school there.

In 1786 he joined the author Engel in managing the royal theatre. Four years later he gave up his professorship and ran the theatre alone until 1796. He died at Berlin in 1798. The entry judges his verse with cool honesty: skilful, but cold and uninspired. His fame rests on his gift for copying classical forms in German. Horace's measures were his chief model. He was also known for correcting his friends' writings past recognition. His cantata The Death of Jesus stayed well known through its musical setting.
britannica-1911-realm: Realm means the lands ruled by a king, or a kingdom. A short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces the word itself. It came into English from an Old French form close to the modern word royaume. The present spelling was not fixed until the start of the 1600s. Scholars link the word to a Latin form built on regalis, meaning of or belonging to a king. That root in turn points to rex, the Latin word for king.
britannica-1911-rustow-friedrich-wilhelm:
Friedrich Wilhelm Rustow, a Swiss soldier and writer on war who lived from 1821 to 1878, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born a Prussian, he served in the army of his own land for some years. A book of his on the German military state drew an official rebuke. A court martial gave him a long term in a fortress, but he escaped to Switzerland.

Rustow won work in Swiss service and by 1857 was a major on the engineer staff. In 1860 he sailed with Garibaldi as colonel and chief of staff for the attack on the two Sicilies. The wins at Capua and at the Volturno are laid to his credit in the text. He then settled at Zurich. Turned down for a new chair of military studies in 1878, he lost heart and took his own life.
britannica-1911-struve-friedrich-georg-w:
Friedrich Georg Wilhelm Struve is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. He was a German star scholar from 1793 to 1864. He was born at Altona in April 1793. His father was Jacob Struve, who died in 1841. In 1808 he entered the school at Dorpat town. He first read word studies there, then turned to stars. From 1813 he taught at that school and watched the skies.

In 1820 he became full teacher and head of the post. He stayed at Dorpat on double stars and land measure. In 1839 he moved to run a new chief star house. That house stood at Pulkowa near Saint Petersburg. He kept at work there till ill health forced rest. He died at Saint Petersburg in November 1864. His name is best known for his work on double stars.
by-reef-and-palm:
Louis Becke, an Australian who traded among Pacific islands, gathered his stories in By Reef and Palm. An introduction recalls Apia in 1870, German traders, and Bully Hayes. Becke had sailed as supercargo, a ship's cargo officer, on Hayes's vessel and shared a shipwreck with him. The tales rest on that island knowledge.

Challis the Doubter opens the set, followed by a story of loyalty among islanders. The Revenge of Macy O'Shea and The Rangers of Tia Kau bring violence and justice to the beaches. Pallou's Taloi, Enderby's Courtship, and Long Charley's Good Little Wife mix love, custom, and comedy. A methodical trader of Majuru, a doctor's wife, and the fate of the Alida round out the volume. Brantley of Vahitahi closes the stories in the islands. Readers of Stevenson and Melville find a rawer Pacific, told by a working trader rather than a tourist.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-culm:
A diocesan entry traces Culm, a bishopric in north-eastern Prussia founded in 1234 and suffragan to Gnesen. Land won by the Teutonic Order on the Vistula and Baltic was divided that year by papal legate William of Modena into four dioceses: Culm, Ermland, Pomesania, and Samland. Innocent IV consecrated the Dominican Heidenreich as first bishop in 1245.

The bishop held the highest spiritual and secular authority in his land, though dependent on the Teutonic Order. His chapter, founded in 1251, joined the Order under his successor. Under the Knights' protection, soil was tilled, inhabitants Christianized, and schools, churches, and courts founded. By 1907 the diocese counted 780,000 Catholics across West Prussia and neighbouring districts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-aldhelm:
St. Aldhelm was abbot of Malmesbury and bishop of Sherborne, Latin poet and church writer, living about 639 to 709. This entry follows a kinsman of Ine, King of Wessex, schooled at Malmesbury under the Irish teacher Maildubh. The town's very name is disputed between Maildubh and Aldhelm himself, perhaps honouring both.

Aldhelm credited his progress in letters to Adrian, the African-born monk of Monte Cassino who came to England with Archbishop Theodore and became abbot of St. Augustine's, Canterbury, though Theodore's arrival in 671 means Aldhelm was already thirty or forty. The entry follows his writings, his abbacy, and his bishopric, presenting a scholar who carried Latin learning into the West Saxon church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-anselm:
St. Anselm was archbishop of Canterbury and a Doctor of the Church. He was born at Aosta, a Burgundian town on the borders of Lombardy. He died on 21 April 1109. This long entry follows a boy who learned his first lessons of piety from his mother, Ermenberga, of an old Burgundian family. His father Gundulf was a Lombard who had become a citizen of Aosta.

As a child Anselm heard his mother speak of God dwelling on high and ruling all things. Living among mountains, he imagined heaven must sit on their lofty summits. One night he dreamed he climbed to the summit and hastened to the court of God, the great King. His biographer Eadmer preserved such childhood memories from Anselm's own lips. The entry follows him from those early visions to the abbacy of Bec and the see of Canterbury, where his writings shaped medieval theology.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stockholm:
Stockholm, capital of Sweden, stands where Lake Mälaren meets a rocky Baltic bay. This entry surveys the city as it stood near 1910. It sketches the islands and heights it is built on, its founding tale under Birger Jarl, and its arms bearing King St Eric.

Trade figures for 1908 show a busy port, with hundreds of factories and tens of thousands of workers. Schools range from the free college founded in 1878 to the Caroline medical institute. Church life gets close attention too, with Catholic numbers, parishes, and the rule that Catholics sought marriage papers from Lutheran pastors. Statistics and sources round out the portrait.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-edmund-br:
Edmund Brindholm, also spelled Bryndeholme, was a martyr and parish priest of Our Lady's at Calais, accused of plotting to betray Calais to the French. The tale ran that Sir Gregory Botolf, chaplain to Lord Lisle, Governor of Calais, had gone to Rome on the business. There he asked the pope to grant Brindholm a living in the English Hospital of St Thomas. Brindholm was about to leave for Rome when he was arrested.

No evidence seems to show he truly joined any plot. Examined on 11 April 1540, he was attainted in that year's Parliament with Clement Philpott of Calais. The charge was adhering to the king's enemy, the Bishop of Rome, and aiding Cardinal Pole in compassing the surprise of Calais. He suffered with Philpott, a victim of Henry VIII's treason laws rather than a proven conspirator, the entry argues.
corea-or-cho-sen-the-land-of-the-morning:
Corea or Cho-sen: The Land of the Morning Calm, by A. Henry Savage Landor, is a travel book dedicated, by gracious permission, to Her Majesty the Queen. Its contents map a journey: Christmas on board, Fusan, a body-snatcher, the Imperatrice Gulf, and Chemulpo. A chapter on the word Corea and a glance at Corean history follow, then the road to Seoul, with its ponies, oxen, coolies, and currency.

Seoul gets its own tour: inns, beggars, an old palace, a leopard hunt, the big bell, sedan chairs, and the Gate of the Dead. Other chapters dress the people by topic: the Coreans' hats and head-bands, the woman of Cho-sen and her privileges and duties, children and their games, kite-flying and spinning-tops among them.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BronsonFilm_Bro:
Charles L. Bronson stood in Dealey Plaza with a movie camera on November 22, 1963, and his film of the assassination slept for years before researchers examined it closely. Earl Golz of the Dallas Morning News reported on it in 1978, when enhanced frames made news.

The enhanced images appeared to show two figures in the Texas School Book Depository's sixth-floor window, where the Warren Commission had placed Oswald alone. If a second figure was real, the lone-gunman account had a problem, and the film became a battleground of photographic experts. Golz's article is the hometown paper covering the evidence debate as it heated up again in the seventies.
malcolm:
Malcolm is a Scottish novel by George MacDonald, set on the Moray coast. Its contents open with Miss Horn and the mad laird. Barbara Catanach, Phemy Mair, and Lady Florimel enter early. The Marquis of Lossie holds the great house above the fisher town.

Malcolm is a fisher lad who works the salmon nets and boats. Duncan MacPhail, a blind Highland piper, stands as his friend and guide. A funeral, a storm, and an accusation test the village. Weddings, revivals, and disclosures crowd the long tale. MacDonald hides a mystery of birth inside the fishing life. His deep faith and poetic heart shine through every chapter.
nasa-tm-19700020670-buoyancy-effects-on-:
S. S. Papell of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for a 1970 cryogenic engineering conference in Boulder, Colorado. It studies how buoyancy affects film boiling of liquid nitrogen in vertical flow. In film boiling, a blanket of vapor wraps the heated surface.

Papell took data for flow moving both upward and downward. The tests ran through an electrically heated tube section. Pressures, inlet speeds, and heat levels all varied across the runs. How buoyant vapor moves against or with the flow changes the boiling. The results matter for cooling systems that carry very cold liquids.
podcast-dannyjones-v76xgCpW5LM:
Researcher Matthew Johnson joins Danny Jones to talk about a new test that uses religious drugs to try to bring God back. Johnson works on DMT and the strange worlds it opens. The test at issue gives the drug in slow, long doses.

Johnson explains how the test is run and what the subjects report at the peak. He asks whether the shared world they find could be a real place where God can be met. Jones presses on faith, fraud, and proof. Listeners get the science and the wonder in one talk. The library files it as an archive record.
podcast-joerogan-EvnLN8WETlM:
Wildlife biologist Forrest Galante joins Joe Rogan for episode 2531 of the Joe Rogan Experience. Galante hosts Extinct or Alive, where he searches for animals thought to be gone forever. His adventures mix science, danger, and genuine discovery in remote places.

Galante tells tales of crocodiles, sharks, and close calls from his expeditions. He explains how his teams confirmed species that science had written off. Rogan, an avid outdoorsman, trades his own stories of the wild. Nature lovers and the brave get a front-row seat to a modern explorer's best missions.
rosmersholm:
Henrik Ibsen wrote Rosmersholm, a play in four acts, here in a translation by R. Farquharson Sharp. John Rosmer, of Rosmersholm, is an ex-clergyman who lives with Rebecca West, first hired as companion to the late Mrs. Rosmer. The cast also holds Kroll, headmaster of the local grammar school and Rosmer's brother-in-law, plus Ulrik Brendel, Peter Mortensgaard, and Mrs. Helseth, the housekeeper. The action takes place at an old manor house near a small town on a fjord in western Norway.

Act 1 opens in the sitting room at Rosmersholm on a summer evening after sunset. The room is large, furnished in old style, with portraits of clergy, officers, and officials on the walls. the-passing-of-new-france-a-chronicle-of:
William Wood wrote The Passing of New France, a chronicle of Montcalm. It is volume 10 of the Chronicles of Canada, edited by George M. Wrong and H. H. Langton, published at Toronto in 1915. Chapter One covers Montcalm in France from 1712 to 1756. It opens with an old family saying: war is the grave of the Montcalms.

Wood traces the family back to the Crusades. Deodat de Gozon became Grand Master of the Knights of St John after devoted service. He won the right to bear the conquered Dragon of Rhodes on the family arms. Montcalm, like Wolfe, was a soldier born. Wood says the badge of victory nerved him to uphold the family tradition in Canada.
